title: The river cut off
hook: at Karbala his camp is surrounded and cut off from the Euphrates

segments.voice: Yesterday, Husayn refuses: a knock at night, a pledge he would not give, and a family setting out across the desert toward Kufa. Your line was: he would not pledge. What small wrong did you say no to? Day eight hundred ninety.

Somewhere on the road to Kufa, the histories say, a troop of horsemen rides up to block Husayn's way. Their commander is al-Hurr. The men have been riding in the heat and they are parched, and so are their horses. Husayn looks at them, and tells his young men to give them water. Give the horses water too. The reports say they filled bowls and held them to the horses' mouths, again and again, until each had drunk. These were the soldiers sent to stop him. A few days later, on a plain by the Euphrates called Karbala, the water would run the other way. Today: the river cut off.
screen: `HORSEMEN BLOCK THE ROAD.` → `GIVE THEM WATER.` → `THE HORSES TOO.`

segments.voice: Kufa does not welcome him. The cousin he sent ahead, Muslim ibn Aqil, has been caught and killed, and the city that wrote all those letters has gone quiet under its new governor, Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad. Husayn is turned aside, and his small camp pitches its tents at Karbala, in the open, near the river. Then a much larger army arrives. And the histories report an order from the governor: put yourselves between Husayn and the water. Do not let them taste a drop. So soldiers line the riverbank. The Euphrates is right there, close enough to see, and the camp, with its children and its women and its old men, cannot reach it. The reports say Husayn's half-brother al-Abbas led a party down to the river by night and fought his way back with some water skins. Shia Muslims remember al-Abbas with deep love as the one who carried water, and the stories of his last attempt are told with great tenderness in Muharram. Keep the detail of the scene in mind: the same camp that had watered its enemies' horses on the road is now refused water by men who have more than enough. The Qur'an says that God made every living thing from water. To cut a family off from a river is to cut at life itself. That is one reason water carries this story in Shia remembrance: a glass offered to a stranger during Muharram can be a memory of Karbala. And it is why the plainest line of this part of the story is also the hardest. They were thirsty.
screen: `KUFA GOES QUIET.` · `TENTS AT KARBALA.` · `BETWEEN HUSAYN AND THE WATER.` · `AL-ABBAS GOES DOWN BY NIGHT.` · then, large: `THEY WERE THIRSTY.`

segments.voice: The practice: drink water thankfully. If you can, pour a glass of water and hold it. Settle, and breathe. Look at it before you drink. Notice how easy it was to get. A tap, a bottle, a few steps. Breathe in. Bring to mind the camp at Karbala, near enough to see the river, unable to reach it. Breathe out. Then drink, slowly, a sip at a time. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you drink and alhamdulillah after. If you don't, just notice each sip. The bell holds the time.
The river cut off. At Karbala, soldiers stood between Husayn's camp and the Euphrates, and a family within sight of water could not drink. Today's word.
Your line: they were thirsty. Today, every time you drink, pause for one breath first. And offer water to someone, even a stranger. Day eight hundred ninety.

howItsDone: In Muharram, Shia Muslims remember the thirst of Husayn's camp at Karbala, and some communities set up stalls to offer water and drinks to passersby in memory of it.

fork.setup: you're Husayn. thirsty horsemen ride up to block your road. you have water. what do you do?
options: keep your water for your own family.
give the men and their horses water.
turn back so you don't have to face them.
fork.reveal: the reports say he had his young men water the soldiers and hold bowls to the horses until each had drunk.

original.note: Arabic: thirst, a word heard often in the elegies of Karbala.

trapdoor: what you thought: Karbala was a battle that happened to be in a desert.
what it means: a family was kept from the Euphrates within sight of it, by an army that had water to spare.
what a scholar hears: al-Tabari's report of the governor's order to hold the river, beside the earlier scene of Husayn watering al-Hurr's horses.

sources.ref: al-Tabari, Tarikh (Husayn waters al-Hurr's men and horses; the death of Muslim ibn Aqil; Ibn Ziyad's order to keep Husayn from the water; al-Abbas's night party to the river)
Qur'an 21:30 (God made every living thing from water)
